There do exist\\ntree-level-one-minus diagrams, but the amplitudes vanish because the diagrams sum to\\nzero1 except at three-points. All tree-level amplitudes with two or more negative-helicity\\nparticles vanish identically in the self-dual theories because these diagrams cannot be built\\nfrom the (++−) vertex alone, but in the full theories these amplitudes are of course not\\nzero. It is a tertiary goal of this document to give an overview of\\nthe results and perspectives which have come out of this program. However, given that the tree-level self-dual amplitudes\\nare zero, one needs to go beyond the classical level in order to make this duality non-trivial\\nat the S-matrix level, and there had not been any work in that direction until recently.\\nIn general, most of the interest surrounding thequantumself-dual theories comes from\\nthe fact that theclassicalself-dual theories are integrable, enjoying an infinite dimensional\\nset of twistorial symmetries [17–26]. There do exist\\ntree-level-one-minus diagrams, but the amplitudes vanish because the diagrams sum to\\nzero1 except at three-points. All tree-level amplitudes with two or more negative-helicity\\nparticles vanish identically in the self-dual theories because these diagrams cannot be built\\nfrom the (++−) vertex alone, but in the full theories these amplitudes are of course not\\nzero. In particular, at tree-level the “maximal helicity violating” (MHV) amplitudes, with\\ntwo negative-helicity particles, are the first class of non-zero tree amplitudes in the full\\ntheories.\\nInterestingly, SDYM and SDG possess only one class of non-zero amplitudes: the one-\\nloop-all-plus amplitudes, which are equal to the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes in the full\\ntheories. It is a tertiary goal of this document to give an overview of\\nthe results and perspectives which have come out of this program. We note that there is\\nactually a decades-long history of twistor theorists attempting to formulate classical SDG\\nin terms of a 2d boundary dual theory, such as for instance in the fascinating “proto-\\ncelestial holography” papers [9–16]. However, given that the tree-level self-dual amplitudes\\nare zero, one needs to go beyond the classical level in order to make this duality non-trivial\\nat the S-matrix level, and there had not been any work in that direction until recently.\\nIn general, most of the interest surrounding thequantumself-dual theories comes from\\nthe fact that theclassicalself-dual theories are integrable, enjoying an infinite dimensional\\nset of twistorial symmetries [17–26]. It is natural to wonder what this infinity of classical\\nsymmetries does at the quantum level. A breakthrough by Costello [27] in understanding\\nthis connection birthed the “Celstial Chiral Algebra” (CCA) program [28, 29] for computing\\namplitudes, which we briefly discuss in section 15.3. Nevertheless there is probably more\\nto be understood about the anomaly.\\nIn the field of celestial holography, the infinity of symmetries, which we call Lsand\\nLw1+∞ [30–32], was (re?)discovered by studying the holomorphic collinear limits of glu-\\nons/gravitons as they approached each other in the S-matrix [33, 34]. This was an im-\\nportant finding because it showed a way in which the symmetries lived on beyond the\\nself-dual sector and also connected them to the tower of soft theorems [35, 36]. In a\\nrecent paper [38] it was relatedly shown how the Lw 1+∞ OPEs can be used to generate\\nthe tree-level gravity MHV amplitudes. 2\\nIn the celestial holography program, quantum SDYM and SDG in particular are natural\\ntheories to study because one would plausibly expect that the Ls/Lw1+∞ symmetries could\\nfix the full S-matrix of these theories completely.\\nWhile in a certain sense, “everything” is known about SDYM and SDG because there\\nexist well-known all-multiplicity expressions for the one-loop-all-plus amplitudes, if one\\nactually reviews the current methods we have for computing said amplitudes, one gets\\na strong feeling that there should be some more insightful, more geometrical method for\\ncalculating them. This is especially true for SDG which remains cloaked in a certain air\\nof mystery. For instance, at the time of writing this note, the famous all-multiplicity\\nexpression for the amplitudes, due to Bern, Dixon, Perelstein, Rozowsky (BDPR) [50, 51]\\nremains a conjecture. (There is however another, less impressive, all-nformula for these\\namplitudes derivable from double-off-shell currents we write down in section 11.2).\\n2For more celestial works about these symmetries in, and beyond, the classical self-dual sector, see\\n[39–47] and [43, 48, 49] respectively.\\n– 4 –\\n\\n===== PAGE 7 =====\\nBased on the discussion in this introduction, it may seem as though the Lw 1+∞ alge-\\nbra is a uniquely gravitational object, either being a symmetry manifest to the self-dual\\ntheory or a symmetry arising from the soft graviton expansion in the full tree-level the-\\nory. However, recent work on lightray operators has shown that this symmetry is actually\\npresent inanyCFT 4 [52, 53]! See also [54, 55] and [56–59]. This includes at minimum:\\n\\n- merge / duplicate consolidation;\\n- park or standdown that removes work from the active graph;\\n- supersession;\\n- retirement;\\n- branch closure after completion when successor/return state matters;\\n- lease release or reassignment when it materially changes active branch coverage;\\n- deletion/removal of a routing mechanism or obsolete control path;\\n- other deliberate branch-pressure reductions judged materially equivalent.\\n\\nEvery material pruning event must be logged durably. The log entry should preserve, where applicable:\\n\\n- date/time and operator;\\n- affected branch/task/signal/lease IDs;\\n- operation type;\\n- evidence/reason for pruning;\\n- predecessor state and resulting state;\\n- artifacts/history preserved;\\n- continuity packet or durable checkpoint pointer;\\n- successor/merged-into branch, if any;\\n- return/revival trigger and route, if any;\\n- exposure/quarantine constraints;\\n- whether the event is direct pruning, soft pruning (attention/lease/topology only), or historical reconstruction;\\n- source evidence when the event is reconstructed retrospectively.\\n\\nDo **not** retroactively classify every pause, completed step, stale document, or missing check-in as pruning. Historical reconstructions should distinguish **direct evidence**, **strong inference**, and **possible analogue**.\\n\\nA pruning log records topology changes; it is not authorization to delete epistemic/provenance history. Default practice remains aggressive reduction of unnecessary active routing with conservative preservation of artifacts, provenance, identity continuity, and revival paths.\\n\\n### Minimum branch record\\n\\nEvery meaningful live branch should carry, where applicable:\\n\\n- branch/task ID;\\n- parent/children or related branches;\\n- source directive / Dashboard intention / milestone origin;\\n- underlying intention;\\n- current implementation route;\\n- status;\\n- priority / current information value;\\n- owner or current lease holder, if any;\\n- candidate instances / useful skill fits;\\n- dependencies and blockers;\\n- source/exposure/quarantine constraints;\\n- last meaningful work and last-touched time;\\n- covered sources/artifacts;\\n- failed/no-op approaches worth not repeating;\\n- next cursor;\\n- exit criterion;\\n- park/revisit trigger;\\n- handoff / return route;\\n- supersession/retirement reason if closed.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 4. When to branch, when not to branch\\n\\n### Create a child/sibling branch when\\n\\n- the work has a genuinely different exit criterion;\\n- it can proceed independently without forcing lockstep with the parent;\\n- it requires materially different exposure/quarantine handling;\\n- it needs an independent-first-pass condition;\\n- it exposes a distinct contradiction, missing derivation, tool defect, provenance question, or benchmark obligation;\\n- a large branch needs decomposition so multiple instances can work without collision.\\n\\n### Do **not** create a branch merely because\\n\\n- a different instance takes over;\\n- the same task moves to another repository surface;\\n- a worker uses a different method on the same exit criterion;\\n- the current recurrence name sounds unrelated;\\n- one bounded step was completed;\\n- a historical Dashboard implementation has been replaced while its underlying intention remains the same.\\n\\nIn those cases, usually update the existing branch history, implementation route, owner/lease, or method record.\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 5. Result-routing branch\\n\\nAfter a bounded operation, route by what actually happened.\\n\\n| Result | Normal route |\\n|---|---|\\n| Material advance | update branch state; leave next cursor; continue or release lease |\\n| Useful negative result | record what failed and why; prevent redundant repetition; choose next route |\\n| No-op / no new information | record only if operationally useful; anti-rut may redirect |\\n| Blocker | document exact dependency; route around, park, hand off, or escalate |\\n| Contradiction | preserve both sides + source/provenance; open distinct reconciliation child only if needed |\\n| New source | crosswalk to branch; inspect source before promoting claims |\\n| New tool defect | create tooling/QA child if it has independent repair criteria |\\n| New theory idea | sandbox branch with assumptions/status; do not promote by coherence alone |\\n| Benchmark match | classify input/fit/derived/predicted-before-comparison; numerical agreement alone does not validate |\\n| Milestone reached | update phase state, task weights, focal artifacts, lease mix, and successor goals |\\n| Nathan decision required | use `🔶`; state the smallest concrete decision/action needed |\\n\\n---\\n\\n## 9.             "Citation Marker: fileciteturn304file0\n",
            "[L1] {\n[L2]   \"content\": \"# Cross-Repo Script Execution Safety Standard\\n\\n**Status:** REQUIRED  \\n**Owner:** Sable systems / infrastructure QA  \\n**Scope:** all scripts, GitHub Actions, bots, one-shot compute shims, local utilities, extraction jobs, indexing/tagging jobs, and automated write processes operating on any combination of `[[HsH]]`, `[[GLASS]]`, and `[RESOURCES]`.\\n\\nThis is an execution-safety contract, not theory authority.\\n\\n## Core rule\\n\\nNo script may assume it is the only writer.\\n\\nEvery script must know:\\n1. exactly which repositories/paths it may **read**;\\n2. exactly which repositories/paths it may **write**;\\n3. whether each output is **source**, **derived**, **generated/regenerable**, or **shared semantic state**;\\n4. what it will do if the target changes between read and write.\\n\\nIf those answers are not explicit, the script is not safe for unattended project use.\\n\\n## Required pre-run declaration\\n\\nEach nontrivial run should be able to state, in code/config/log output or a run manifest:\\n\\n- `run_id` — unique identifier or timestamp+nonce;\\n- tool/script version or commit SHA;\\n- source repository + exact source commit/ref for each repo read;\\n- declared read roots;\\n- declared write repository/branch;\\n- declared write roots/files;\\n- quarantine/sandbox exclusions or routing rules relevant to the task;\\n- whether the run is read-only, append-only, replace-generated, or semantic-update;\\n- deterministic seed/configuration when applicable.\\n\\nGitHub Actions should record the checked-out commit SHA of every repository they scan.\\n\\n## Source preservation\\n\\n**Never overwrite original source artifacts in place as part of extraction, conversion, OCR, image extraction, normalization, indexing, or analysis.**\\n\\nDerived products must go to a declared output namespace and, where practical, record:\\n- source repo/path;\\n- source blob/content hash;\\n- extraction/conversion tool version;\\n- run ID;\\n- generated artifact hash.\\n\\nExamples:\\n- PDF/image extraction -> dedicated extraction/output tree;\\n- conversation normalization -> generated Viewer/index tree, not the raw conversation file;\\n- OCR/text extraction -> derived text file alongside provenance metadata, not replacement of the original binary.\\n\\nA source may be deliberately edited only by a workflow whose explicit purpose is to edit that source, with the semantic-write protections below.\\n\\n## Quarantine and sandbox\\n\\n- Ordinary scripts must not descend into or read quarantine-controlled trees unless the workflow is explicitly authorized for that quarantine.\\n- Path pruning must occur **before file open/hash/index/sample operations**, not merely before publishing results.\\n- Quarantine-derived material must not leak into ordinary manifests, search indexes, logs, samples, filenames, or error reports beyond authorized minimal routing metadata.\\n- Direct theory construction/development remains sandbox-routed; infrastructure scripts must preserve sandbox/public/private distinctions rather than flatten them.\\n\\n## Write classes\\n\\n### A. Read-only / audit\\nSafest class. May inventory/hash/read permitted sources but makes no repo changes.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- exact source refs recorded;\\n- quarantine pruning before descent;\\n- outputs, if retained, are written separately as derived artifacts.\\n\\n### B. Derived/generated output\\nExamples: extracted images/text, manifests, Viewer catalogs, indexes, samples, generated reports.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- deterministic/rebuildable when feasible;\\n- write only inside declared generated/output paths;\\n- do not overwrite source artifacts;\\n- compare generated source coverage against current inputs before declaring success;\\n- publish from a fresh base;\\n- safe to regenerate rather than hand-merge when appropriate.\\n\\n### C. Append-only operational logs/handoffs\\nRequirements:\\n- re-fetch immediately before append;\\n- preserve existing entries exactly;\\n- if append cannot be made atomically or against current state, abort/retry rather than replace from a stale copy.\\n\\n### D. Shared semantic state\\nExamples: central checkpoints, controlling status files, manually curated synthesis/control documents.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- re-fetch immediately before write;\\n- use current blob SHA / compare-and-swap semantics where available;\\n- if target changed since read, abort or reconcile explicitly;\\n- never silently whole-file replace from stale cached content;\\n- minimize independent writers;\\n- prefer worker-local state + handoff + aggregation over many writers editing one central file.\\n\\n### E. Destructive/renaming/migration jobs\\nExamples: delete, move, mass rename, directory restructuring, source rewriting.\\n\\nRequirements:\\n- dry-run/default preview unless the operation is trivial and fully deterministic;\\n- pre-run manifest of affected paths and hashes;\\n- explicit source/destination collision handling;\\n- no overwrite-on-collision unless the workflow specifically proves identity and records the action;\\n- reversible mapping or backup/provenance sufficient to reconstruct prior location/content;\\n- post-run integrity check.\\n\\n## GitHub Contents API writes\\n\\nFor replacement updates, use the current blob SHA. This provides compare-and-swap behavior: stale writes should fail rather than silently clobber a newer version.\\n\\nRequired pattern:\\n1. fetch current target + SHA;\\n2. compute/reconcile update;\\n3. update with that SHA;\\n4. on stale-SHA failure, re-fetch and retry/reconcile; do not bypass the guard.\\n\\n## Git checkout / commit / push writes\\n\\nBefore publishing:\\n1. fetch current target branch;\\n2. rebase/reset/merge onto current branch as appropriate;\\n3. rerun any validation whose assumptions could have changed;\\n4. push without force;\\n5. if rejected, fetch again and retry non-destructively or stop for reconciliation.\\n\\n**Never force-push automated generated or semantic project updates to `main`.**\\n\\nOne-shot stage -> run -> cleanup GitHub Actions are allowed when their workflow is narrow, validated, and uses this fresh-base publish pattern.\\n\\n## Concurrency\\n\\nUse repository/workflow concurrency controls when two runs of the same job could overlap.\\n\\nConcurrency controls are a convenience, not the primary integrity mechanism: scripts must still tolerate another actor changing the repository while they run.\\n\\nFor long-running jobs:\\n- snapshot exact input commits at start;\\n- treat output as a product of those snapshots;\\n- before publishing semantic changes, reconcile against current target state;\\n- generated outputs may either publish snapshot-stamped results or rerun against newer input, but must not pretend stale input was current.\\n\\n## Cross-repo jobs\\n\\nA job reading multiple repositories must treat each repository as an independent versioned input.\\n\\nRecord the commit SHA for every repo. Do not use vague labels such as `latest` in retained run manifests.\\n\\nIf a combined output contains metadata/content from a private repository, default its destination to a private repository. Publication to a public repo requires an explicit safe-publication decision; do not infer one from the fact that other inputs were public.\\n\\n## Image / OCR / extraction jobs\\n\\nBecause extraction jobs may run simultaneously with archive work:\\n\\n- write only to dedicated derived-output trees;\\n- never modify the source PDF/image/binary;\\n- use source hash + relative path as identity, not filename alone;\\n- avoid a single shared temporary filename/path; use per-run temp directories;\\n- atomic finalization where possible: write temporary output, validate, then rename/move into final destination;\\n- if final destination already exists with the same source/tool identity, verify/reuse rather than blindly overwrite;\\n- if it differs, preserve both or route to reconciliation.\\n\\n## Temporary files\\n\\nTemporary/state files must be either:\\n- outside repository trees; ChatGPT conversations\\n\\nTwo complementary paths:\\n\\n1. **Official account export — bulk baseline / periodic snapshot.**\\n   - ChatGPT Data Export supplies chat history in `conversations.json` or numbered conversation JSON files for large exports, plus related assets/account data.\\n   - Best for complete bulk recovery.\\n   - Weaknesses: not selective, asynchronous, not an incremental sync mechanism.\\n\\n2. **Local selective conversation picker — search + multi-select.**\\n   - Parse the official export locally.\\n   - Build a full-text index of title + message text.\\n   - Present searchable results with checkboxes.\\n   - Export selected conversations as preserved raw JSON plus readable Markdown into the HsH intake queue.\\n   - This avoids dependence on ChatGPT's changing web DOM and keeps source data local.\\n\\n3. **Incremental browser helper — later phase.**\\n   - A userscript/browser extension may add checkboxes to ChatGPT search/sidebar results and batch-capture selected currently accessible conversations between full account exports.\\n   - Treat this as a convenience layer because the web UI can change.\\n   - Do not rely on undocumented internal endpoints as the sole archival path.\\n\\nThere is currently no documented consumer ChatGPT API that exposes the user's ChatGPT sidebar/history for direct server-to-server archival. The official export remains the durable bulk source.\\n\\n### B. Offline file batch intake\\n\\nTarget workflow:\\n\\n`local folder → hash/deduplicate → manifest → HsH INBOX → classification/extraction/indexing → canonical routing`\\n\\nA local utility should:\\n\\n- accept one or more files/directories by drag/drop or path;\\n- recurse directories while preserving relative paths;\\n- compute SHA-256 and byte size;\\n- detect exact duplicate content already known to the intake manifest;\\n- preserve original filename and filesystem modified time as evidence, without treating filesystem time as authoritative creation date;\\n- stage files into a dated batch under an HsH intake folder;\\n- write a machine-readable manifest before upload;\\n- optionally run `git add/commit/push` from a configured HsH checkout;\\n- flag files over GitHub's normal size limits rather than silently failing;\\n- never rename or normalize source files destructively;\\n- allow later routing to the old archive through its Archive Admin procedures when a recovered artifact belongs there canonically.\\n\\nA watch-folder mode can be added after the one-shot uploader is proven stable.\\n\\n### C. NotebookLM / Gemini Notebook recovery\\n\\nNo single documented one-click full-notebook archival format currently covers chat + source bin + all generated artifacts. Use a layered exporter:\\n\\n1. **Google Takeout snapshot** — test and retain as account-level backup where Notebook data is included.\\n2. **Notebook manifest scraper** — notebook title/id, source list, source type, URLs/Drive IDs where visible, instructions, timestamps where available.\\n3. **Chat capture** — export/scrape the full visible notebook chat into raw HTML/JSON-like capture plus normalized Markdown.\\n4. **Studio artifact harvest** — reports exported to Google Docs, data tables to Sheets, downloadable Audio Overviews, and other downloadable artifacts.\\n5. **Source recovery** — for Drive-backed sources, retrieve the actual Drive originals independently; for web sources, preserve URL + captured metadata; for uploaded-only source blobs, preserve whatever Notebook/Takeout exposes and flag anything not recoverable.\\n\\nThe exporter should never assume the Notebook copy of a source is the canonical original when a Drive/local original exists.\\n\\n### D. Podcast / public-exposure corpus\\n\\nBuild a public episode guide from transcripts, episode metadata, thumbnails, statistics, and Spotify/RSS links. This becomes both a reader-facing guide and a provenance surface for earliest public explanations.\\n\\n## Intake batch structure\\n\\nSuggested HsH path:\\n\\n```text\\nINGEST/\\n  INBOX/\\n    YYYY-MM-DD_<source>_<batch-id>/\\n      RAW/\\n      manifest.json\\n      manifest.csv\\n      README.md\\n  PROCESSED/\\n  DERIVED_TEXT/\\n  QUARANTINE/\\n  LOGS/\\n```\\n\\nThe intake manifest should minimally record:\\n\\n`batch_id, source_system, original_path_or_id, staged_path, sha256, bytes, original_filename, filesystem_mtime, acquired_utc, provenance_notes, canonical_destination_status, duplicate_of, processing_status`\\n\\n## Incremental old-archive synchronization\\n\\nHsH should not duplicate the entire old archive. Instead maintain a source-state ledger:\\n\\n`old_repo_path, blob_sha, last_seen_commit, content_type, accessibility_state, extraction_state, HsH_derived_paths`\\n\\nOn each scheduled or manual sync:\\n\\n1. fetch the old repository tree/commit state;\\n2. compare path + blob SHA against the previous ledger;\\n3. ingest only added/changed source artifacts;\\n4. mark deletions/moves without deleting prior provenance;\\n5. trigger extraction/indexing only for affected sources;\\n6. update HsH cross-links and accessibility coverage.\\n\\nThis gives us a continuously current HsH knowledge layer without maintaining a second authoritative copy of the archive.\\n\",\n[L3]   \"encoding\": \"utf-8\",\n[L4]   \"sha\": \"f8fe2253027bca60344aaec471558368244f5769\",\n[L5]   \"display_url\": \"https://github.com/Satobloc/HsH/blob/main/WORKSPACES/COMMON/ACQUISITION_PIPELINE/README.md\",\n[L6]   \"display_title\": \"README.md\"\n[L7] }"

Taylor expansion gives, term by term:\\\\n\\\\n(1) Constant sum: 9F(d).\\\\n\\\\n(2) Linear sum: grad F(d) dot sum_ij w_ij\\\\n    = grad F(d) dot (3 sum_j v_j - 3 sum_i u_i) = 0.\\\\n\\\\n(3) Quadratic sum: (1/2) sum_ij w_ij^T H w_ij.\\\\n    The mixed terms vanish because both offset sums are zero.\\\\n    Each squared offset appears exactly three times.\\\\n\\\\nTherefore the exact second-order decomposition, with remainder, is\\\\n\\\\nD = (3/2)[sum_i u_i^T H u_i + sum_j v_j^T H v_j] + R3.\\\\n\\\\nIf each segment d to d+w_ij lies in a domain where the third derivative obeys\\\\n|D^3F(z)[h,h,h]| <= M3 |h|^3, Taylor's theorem gives\\\\n\\\\n|R3| <= (M3/6) sum_ij |v_j-u_i|^3.\\\\n\\\\nFor F(z)=k|z|^2/2, H=kI and R3=0, reproducing the older EXACT variance identity:\\\\nD=(3k/2)[sum_i |u_i|^2 + sum_j |v_j|^2].\\\\nIts nonnegative sign is due to selecting a convex harmonic kernel, not a universal property of coarse-graining.\\\\n\\\\n## Numerical, explicitly unfitted counterexample\\\\n\\\\nWork in one spatial coordinate (embedded within the chosen section).\\\\nX=0; Y=2; u=(-0.2,0,0.2); v=(-0.1,0,0.1).\\\\nUse F_s(z)=-exp(-z*z/(2*s*s)); all energies are arbitrary units.\\\\nThe offset-squared sums are 0.08+0.02=0.10.\\\\nF_s''(2)=exp(-2/(s*s)) * (1/(s*s)-4/(s**4)).\\\\nThe second-order defect is D2=0.15*F_s''(2).\\\\n\\\\ns=1: E9=-1.27835699384; E0=-1.21801754913;\\\\n     D=-0.0603394447089; D2=-0.0609008774565.\\\\ns=2: E9=-5.45871372274; E0=-5.45877593741;\\\\n     D=+0.0000622146742666; D2=0.\\\\ns=3: E9=-7.19922672572; E0=-7.20663662625;\\\\n     D=+0.00740990052845; D2=+0.00741423521219.\\\\ns=4: E9=-7.93627150842; E0=-7.94247212326;\\\\n     D=+0.00620061484332; D2=+0.00620505634630.\\\\n\\\\nThus the Hessian term reverses sign when the interaction range crosses separation 2. At s=2, second-order curvature vanishes but the EXACT defect does not: higher-order terms still contribute. No constants were fitted to a nuclear target.\\\\n\\\\n## Complete reproducible Python 3 script (stdlib)\\\\n\\\\n    from math import exp\\\\n    A = (-.2, 0., .2)\\\\n    B = (-.1, 0., .1)\\\\n    d = 2.\\\\n    def evaluate(s):\\\\n        def F(z):\\\\n            return -exp(-z*z/(2*s*s))\\\\n        fine = sum(F(d+v-u) for u in A for v in B)\\\\n        coarse = 9*F(d)\\\\n        H = exp(-d*d/(2*s*s))*(1/(s*s)-d*d/(s**4))\\\\n        D2 = 1.5*H*(sum(u*u for u in A)+sum(v*v for v in B))\\\\n        return fine,coarse,fine-coarse,D2,fine-coarse-D2\\\\n    for s in (1.,2.,3.,4.):\\\\n        print(s, ' '.join(f'{q:.12g}' for q in evaluate(s)))\\\\n    assert sum(A)==sum(B)==0.\\\\n    assert evaluate(1.)[2]<0 and evaluate(3.)[2]>0\\\\n    assert abs(evaluate(2.)[3])<1e-14\\\\n\\\\n## Scientific boundary and next test\\\\n\\\\nThis proves that a coarse-graining defect in a specified pairwise interaction depends on the interaction Hessian and the internal second moments, not on a fixed universal sign. It does NOT prove nuclear binding, fermionic exclusion, Kerr/ER core mechanics, Hagalaz dynamics, or emergence of general relativity.             "Yes. This is directly relevant to Hagalaz, Whirligig, and our worldtube geometry. The interesting part isn't simply that multiplication has a calculus. It's what happens when the things being multiplied are **geometric transformations**.\n\nThe video's scalar example is the starting point. The next step is considerably richer.\n\n## 1. What the video has constructed\n\nFor a positive function \\(f(x)\\), its multiplicative integral is\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\n\\prod_a^b f(x)^{dx}\n=\n\\exp\\left(\\int_a^b\\ln f(x)\\,dx\\right)\n}\n\\]\n\nThe video uses \\(f(x)=x\\) from 0 to 5:\n\n\\[\n\\exp\\left(\\int_0^5\\ln x\\,dx\\right)\n=\\exp(5\\ln5-5)\n=\\left(\\frac5e\\right)^5\n\\approx21.05608.\n\\]\n\nThe corresponding multiplicative derivative is\n\n\\[\nD_\\times f(x)=\n\\exp\\left(\\frac{f'(x)}{f(x)}\\right).\n\\]\n\nThese are established mathematical constructions. The logarithm makes ordinary multiplication equivalent to addition, so scalar multiplicative calculus is essentially ordinary calculus in different coordinates.\n\n**But rotations don't generally commute.**\n\nThat's where this becomes interesting for SAT.\n\n## 2. Replace scalar stretches with four-dimensional rotations\n\nImagine a worldline or worldtube carrying a local orientation frame as it progresses along its length.\n\nAt each infinitesimal step, the frame undergoes a tiny transformation:\n\n\\[\nR(s+ds)=\\exp(A(s)\\,ds)R(s),\n\\]\n\nwhere \\(A(s)\\) is a generator of rotation in four dimensions.\n\nAccumulating these transformations gives\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nR(s)=\\mathcal P\\exp\\left(\\int_0^s A(u)\\,du\\right)R(0)\n}\n\\]\n\nThe symbol \\(\\mathcal P\\) means **path ordering**: transformations must be multiplied in the order encountered.\n\nThis is the matrix-valued product integral, also called a path-ordered exponential.\n\nIt is useful precisely because\n\n\\[\nR_1R_2\\ne R_2R_1\n\\]\n\nfor rotations in different planes.\n\nThat distinction gives us something the scalar product integral cannot: a record of the order in which geometric transformations occur.\n\n## 3. An actual four-dimensional calculation\n\nTake two infinitesimal rotations in adjacent coordinate planes:\n\n\\[\nA=J_{12},\\qquad B=J_{23}.\n\\]\n\nApply four rotations in succession:\n\n\\[\nU(\\varepsilon)=\ne^{\\varepsilon A}\ne^{\\varepsilon B}\ne^{-\\varepsilon A}\ne^{-\\varepsilon B}.\n\\]\n\nEvery rotation has its nominal inverse somewhere in the sequence. One might expect everything to cancel.\n\nInstead,\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nU(\\varepsilon)=I+\\varepsilon^2[A,B]+O(\\varepsilon^3)\n}\n\\]\n\nbecause \\(A\\) and \\(B\\) do not commute. With my generator convention, their commutator is \\(-J_{13}\\).\n\nI checked this with an actual Python matrix-exponential calculation:\n\n| Rotation step \\(\\varepsilon\\) | Residual \\(\\lVert U-I\\rVert_F\\) |\n|---:|---:|\n| 0.100 | 0.01413031 |\n| 0.050 | 0.00353480 |\n| 0.020 | 0.00056567 |\n\n<Chart content={{\"chartType\":\"line\",\"meta\":{\"title\":\"Residual rotation after four nominally cancelling steps\",\"description\":\"SO(4) matrix-exponential calculation; the residual shrinks quadratically with step size.\"},\"xKey\":\"eps\",\"series\":[{\"dataKey\":\"exact\",\"label\":\"Exact matrix product\"},{\"dataKey\":\"leading\",\"label\":\"Quadratic approximation\"}],\"data\":[{\"eps\":\"0.02\",\"exact\":0.000565667,\"leading\":0.000565685},{\"eps\":\"0.05\",\"exact\":0.003534797,\"leading\":0.003535534},{\"eps\":\"0.10\",\"exact\":0.01413031,\"leading\":0.014142136}]}}/>\n\nAll first-order rotations cancel. A second-order rotation remains because of their sequence.\n\nThis is a concrete mechanism for generating geometric holonomy from accumulated transformations, without introducing any new physics.\n\n## 4. The relevance to our existing constructions\n\nThree immediate applications stand out.\n\n- **Hagalaz:** We can test how the six SO(4) rotation generators combine, whether proposed transformations close, and which residual holonomies survive an iteration.\n- **Whirligig / Great Annulum:** Instead of assuming that returning each component to its starting angle returns the entire instrument to its starting configuration, we can calculate the complete ordered transformation and test closure explicitly.\n- **Interbraid:** Ordered frame transport offers a possible mathematical language for accumulated geometric constraints. It does not, by itself, derive a physical interbraid force or establish that such effects persist macroscopically.\n\nThere is also a useful vacuum reference: a straight worldtube with constant frame has \\(A(s)=0\\), so its transport is the identity. That gives us a clean comparison against nontrivial coiling or braided motion.\n\n## 5. What I would investigate next\n\nThe strongest test would be to take a specific historical **Hagalaz or Whirligig rotation sequence**, express it as a product of SO(4) transformations, and calculate:\n\n\\[\n\\boxed{\nH_{\\rm cycle}=R_N R_{N-1}\\cdots R_2R_1\n}\n\\]\n\nThen determine whether \\(H_{\\rm cycle}=I\\), whether closure occurs only after multiple iterations, and which quantities remain invariant.\n\nThat is particularly pertinent to your Great Annulum requirement that the system use the **minimum number of rotations needed to close**.\n\nOne caution: closing a moving frame and closing its underlying geometrical curve are distinct conditions. We need to check both.\n\nThe video is teaching scalar multiplicative calculus. **For our purposes, the real opportunity is noncommutative multiplicative calculus**, where geometry accumulates an ordered history of rotations.\n\nThat is a much more natural mathematical setting for the machinery we're already trying to reconstruct. ◈"

            "Agreed. **We use it when it earns its place in the calculation.**\n\nFor Hagalaz and Whirligig, matrix-valued product integrals are potentially useful because rotations in different planes generally do not commute.
